slides.title: Priorities: Individual Quarterly Priorities
slides.headline: Priorities: Individual Quarterly Priorities
notes: Individual priorities turn the QHAG into each person’s commitments for the quarter.
This is the last step of the cascade: every priority traces back to the BHAG.
slides.support: Each person’s step toward the QHAG.
body: Commit to the few priorities that deliver the QHAG. Each has an owner, a done-by date and a measure of success.

artwork.alt: The cascade from BHAG to priorities: BHAG, 3HAG, 1HAG, QHAG, then individual quarterly priorities. Each level is built from the one above it and directs the one below. Priorities is highlighted: this is where we are.

slides.title: What are your priorities for the quarter?
slides.headline: What are your priorities for the quarter?
notes: Start with the owner of company priority #1, then the other company-priority owners.
Each owner places that commitment first in their individual plan. Add other aligned work and a development commitment.

Allow up to five work priorities and one development priority. Two that are delivered beat five that are started. When capacity conflicts, the company priority wins. Protect enough time for real discussion.
Include every company priority you own. Do not drop one because you own several.
Leaders without an owned company priority identify the aligned work they must deliver. Keep all commitments within capacity.
Run the six questions from the “Pick the priorities that contribute most to success” slide on each individual priority. Hover over “six questions” to show them.

Critical number: it heads each person’s column, above their priorities. It can be financial or not. A widget, what the function hands to the next one, is the better choice. Ask: did I have a good day? A person who owns two functions has one for each.
At a quarterly, start from the critical number you named for your function on the Team View.
At a quarterly, list your open priorities from last quarter first. They stay until their number has moved.

panels.heading: Critical number
panels.support: The one number you own that tells you whether you had a good day. One for each function you own.

panels.heading: Up to 5 work priorities
panels.support: Two delivered beat five started. A company priority you own goes first and wins if time runs short. Test each with the six questions. Add a done-by date and a measure of success.

panels.heading: Professional development
panels.support: Add a skill or behavior to develop, beyond the 5 work priorities.

tip: What does it build or move?
How much will it move a critical number?
How soon will we see it?
Who can own it and succeed?

slides.title: Read your commitments to the team.
slides.headline: Read your commitments to the team.
notes: Before the read-back starts, the team names company priority #1 and its owner. If it is not named, go back to the “What is the #1 priority for the quarter?” slide.
Each person reads their critical number. Then they read each priority with its done-by date, measure and achieved-by date, then their professional development.
Peers ask about missing work, dependencies and assumed handoffs. Resolve gaps and overlaps.
Challenge whether the commitments fit the quarter’s capacity. This exercise can take an hour.

artwork.alt: A leader presents commitments while peers review the shared plan.

body: Name company priority #1 and its owner. They go first.
Read your critical number, priorities and professional development.
Peers ask: can you get all that done?

slides.title: Does your plan pass?
slides.headline: Does your plan pass?
body: Every number and priority has one owner with capacity.
The 1HAG and the QHAG each have ideally 3, up to 5 priorities.
Every priority has a done-by date, a measure of success and an achieved-by date.
Each 1HAG priority builds a 3HAG capability or moves a KFFM lever.
Each QHAG priority advances a 1HAG priority.
Each individual priority supports a QHAG priority or the owner’s critical number.
Each priority moves its number enough, and soon enough to see.
The 1HAG targets reach the 3HAG, and the QHAG targets keep the 1HAG on track.
The widget targets support the revenue.
Head count is set on the 1HAG and QHAG.
notes: Run this as the final read-back, top of the board to bottom.
Do the widget volumes, conversion rates and prices support the revenue target? Which assumption explains any gap?
Anything that fails goes on the homework list with an owner.

At a quarterly, check that each Market Map circle has a home. It becomes a 3HAG capability, a KFFM change or a priority, or the team drops it. Check that last quarter’s open priorities are on the new QHAG.
